definition: The quality of being correct or exact and free from mistakes.
example: The lab technicians calibrate their scales every morning to ensure the accuracy of each measurement.
nuance: Accuracy means getting close to the true value; precision means results are consistent or finely detailed, even if they are wrong.
prompt: A newspaper reporter checks a story the night before it is printed.
options: She phoned each source to confirm the accuracy of every quote in the story.
Her editor praised the story's accuracy because she turned it in an hour early.
The story's accuracy was obvious from the many misspelled names in it.
The story had great accuracy because it filled four whole pages of the paper.
reasons: Checking quotes against their sources is how a reporter makes sure nothing is wrong.
Finishing early is about speed, which says nothing about whether the facts are right.
Misspelled names are errors, so they show the reverse of correctness.
A long article can still be full of mistakes; length does not measure correctness.

practice.prompt: An archer practices at a target on a windy afternoon.
options: Her accuracy impressed the coach, since her arrows scattered far from the target.
Her accuracy came from firing as many arrows per minute as she possibly could.
Thanks to her accuracy, she could pull the bowstring back farther than anyone else.
Once she aimed slightly into the wind, her accuracy improved and most arrows struck the center.
reasons: Arrows landing far from the mark are misses, the opposite of hitting the target.
Shooting fast is a matter of speed, and rushing usually makes shots less exact.
Drawing a bow farther takes strength, which is different from hitting what you aim at.
Arrows landing where she aimed show that her shots were on target.
